content: Multilingual support for East Asian languages, such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, is integrated into relevant articles on Wikipedia. However, computers running English or other Western or Cyrillic operating systems may require additional configuration to properly display these characters. If these characters are not rendered correctly, the issue is referred to as mojibake in Japanese. To verify if your system supports East Asian characters, check if you see boxes, question marks, or nonsensical letters instead of the intended characters. If this occurs, your system lacks the necessary support. For older Windows systems like Windows 95, 98, ME, and NT, you need to download and install the Microsoft Global Input Method Editors (IMEs) for the specific language(s) you require. IMEs enable input of Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) characters, while language packs provide the character sets needed for display. If you are using Office XP, you must install a newer version of the IMEs, as the older versions are incompatible. Sometimes, your system may prompt you to download Asian fonts automatically when viewing pages in these languages. If not, you can manually update your system with the required language support packs. For Windows 2000, XP, and Server 2003, the installation of East Asian language support requires the Windows installation CD-ROM. However, for Windows XP Media Center Edition (MCE), the CD-ROM may not be necessary, as some systems (e.g., eMachines) include Asian fonts on the hard drive but do not install them by default. Windows Vista natively supports East Asian characters. For earlier versions of macOS, you needed to install Language Kits from Apple to read Chinese, Japanese, or Korean on the internet. These kits included WorldScript software, which provided encoding support for specific language character sets. Each language required a separate script. In more recent versions of macOS, these Language Kits are included by default. Once installed, you can select the desired language character set for internet pages via the browser's encoding or character set settings. GNOME and KDE desktop environments natively support East Asian characters, but you may need to install appropriate fonts. For KDE, you might need to install specific packages, such as `kde-i18n-ja` for Japanese. If some characters are still missing, you can use `qtconfig` to add a comprehensive Unicode font to your browser's font substitutions. For Debian GNU/Linux, you must install font packages to display Chinese, Japanese, and Korean characters. Examples include: Traditional Chinese (Big5): `ttf-arphic-bkai00mp` Simplified Chinese (GB): `ttf-arphic-gbsn00lp` Korean: `ttf-baekmuk` Japanese: `ttf-kochi-mincho` After installing these packages, restart the X server to apply the changes. For Fedora Linux, install the appropriate `ttfonts` packages. For example: Traditional Chinese: `ttfonts-zh_TW` Simplified Chinese: `ttfonts-zh_CN` Japanese: `ttfonts-ja` Korean: `ttfonts-ko` In Fedora Core 3, you can use the `yum` command to install these fonts (e.g., `yum install ttfonts-ko`). For Fedora 7 and later versions, the packages are named `fonts-Japanese`, `fonts-Chinese`, and `fonts-Korean`. For Gentoo Linux, enabling the `cjk` (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) USE flag enhances East Asian support in some packages but is not mandatory. Useful font packages include `cjkuni-fonts`, `arphicfonts` (for Chinese), `baekmuk-fonts` (for Korean), and `kochi-substitute` (for Japanese). To install a new font, download it (e.g., in `.ttf` format), copy it to `/usr/lib/X11/fonts/TTF/` (as root), and then run `/usr/X11/bin/fc-cache /usr/lib/X11/fonts/TTF/` (also as root). Restart the X server to apply the changes, and the new font should be available.
